html:
The Battle of the Dunes was fought on 14 June 1658 on the sand dunes east of Dunkirk, on the Channel coast of today's northern France. A French army under Marshal Turenne, with English allies, beat a Spanish army that had come to relieve the town.

France and Spain had been at war since 1635, and their fight outlasted the Thirty Years' War. In 1657 France made an alliance with the English republic of Oliver Cromwell, which sent 6,000 soldiers and a fleet in return for Dunkirk, then a Spanish port. Turenne besieged the town. The Spanish army that marched to save it included the Great Condé, the French prince who had won at Rocroi and then rebelled, and English royalists under the future James II. Turenne attacked as the tide went out, so that his cavalry could ride along the beach and around the Spanish flank. The English foot stormed the highest dune.

Dunkirk surrendered and was handed to England, which sold it to France in 1662. Spain made peace in 1659 in the Treaty of the Pyrenees. The treaty marks the rise of France as the leading power in Europe under Louis XIV.
